after: ## Why sources matter so much in this essay
alt: Range: sources from more than one place, type and standpoint. Assessment: an informed judgement of how far each source can be trusted, answering “how good is this source?”. Justification: why each key source belongs, answering “why have I used it here?”.
caption: Assessing asks how good a source is; justifying asks why it is in your essay.

after: ## What a "range" of sources looks like
alt: Geographical range means sources from more than one region; type range means a mix of academic research, official data, organisational reports and quality journalism; standpoint range means each perspective has a source arguing for it in its own terms. Six sources used and evaluated beat fifteen mentioned once.
caption: Check your list for place, type and standpoint, not just length.

after: ## Choosing sources that "offer firmly supported judgements"
alt: Each candidate source passes four checks: does it give reasons and evidence or only assertions, can its evidence be traced, is the writer qualified to judge, and does it address the question rather than a neighbouring one. Sources that pass reach firmly supported judgements through visible evidence.
caption: Prefer sources whose reasoning and evidence you can see and check.

after: ## Keeping a source audit while you research
alt: An audit table with seven columns for each source: reference, perspective, provenance, basis, strength, limitation and use. The final Use column, what the source will do in the essay, is highlighted as the justification.
caption: Write the evaluation as you read; the Use column is your justification.

after: ## Assessing a source inside your argument
alt: Three techniques with example wording: an evaluative clause attached to the citation, a comparison of credibility when two sources disagree, and a limit that changes how much weight a finding gets.
caption: Put the judgement where the source is used, and make it change something.

after: ## Worked example: weak and strong use of the same sources
alt: For a question on congestion charges, the weak paragraph cites sources but assesses none and calls them all reliable. The strong paragraph assesses the transport authority’s interest against its checkable data, justifies relying more on an independent three-continent study, and uses range across both.
caption: A strong paragraph assesses, justifies and shows range in the same few sentences.

alt: The title, references and citations are not counted in the word limit, but the argument and evaluative sentences about sources are. A sentence or two of evaluation per key source is realistic; a paragraph for every source is not.
caption: References are free; evaluation costs words, so ration it to key sources.
